transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, thanks. Um… I guess what finally pushed me to make the appointment is this thing where I keep getting up at really bad times, even when I absolutely know I should just stay seated and pay attention.

Like at work, I’m a software developer, and during sprint planning—which is already kind of a lot, because everyone’s talking through tickets and priorities—I’ll suddenly be like, “I need water,” or I’ll remember something I want to check in the other room. And I know it’s not a good moment to leave, but I do it anyway. Or on mortgage calls, which are obviously important and kind of serious, I’ll still find myself getting up, walking around, going to check something, grabbing something unnecessary… and then I’m half-listening from another room.

It sounds small when I say it out loud, but it’s started to feel embarrassing and disruptive. Like, I’m 40, I should be able to sit through a meeting or a phone call without inventing reasons to leave the chair. That’s the main thing that made me think, okay, maybe I should actually talk to someone about this.

Thinking back, did you notice this same kind of restlessness or trouble staying seated and focused when you were a kid, say in grade school, or is this something that's really only shown up in adulthood?

Yeah, it was definitely there when I was a kid too. I mean, I don’t have, like, a perfect memory of every grade, but I do remember in elementary school teachers moving my desk or putting me closer to them, or sort of off to the side, because I’d keep popping up out of my seat.

And it wasn’t that I didn’t understand the work, necessarily. Sometimes I understood it fine, but I’d rush through it or get ahead of myself. Or I’d talk before I was called on—like I’d know the answer and just blurt it out—and then get reminded to raise my hand or wait my turn. I remember a lot of “please sit down,” “stay in your seat,” that kind of thing.

At the time I think it was framed as me being chatty or impatient or just needing to calm down, so I didn’t really think of it as anything bigger. But looking back, yeah, the whole restless, can’t-quite-stay-put thing was not new in adulthood.

When you feel the urge to get up and move during these meetings or calls, is it usually accompanied by worried or anxious thoughts running through your mind, or does it happen even when you're not feeling particularly anxious?

It happens even when I’m not especially anxious. I mean, sometimes meetings are stressful in the normal way, sure, but the getting-up thing doesn’t feel like, “Oh no, something bad is going to happen,” or like my thoughts are spiraling.

It’s more physical than that, I think. Like even if I look calm sitting there, inside there’s this building pressure, like I need to move or switch to something else or at least do something with my hands. If I try to just sit still and force myself to listen, it can feel almost like I’m crawling out of my skin a little. Not dramatically, but enough that getting up or fidgeting or grabbing something feels like a relief.

So, yeah—there can be anxious moments, but the urge to move isn’t only when I’m worried. It happens even when I’m mentally fine, just… restless inside.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a lifelong (since elementary school) pattern of motor restlessness, difficulty remaining seated during structured tasks (meetings, calls), impulsive blurting out of answers, and an internal physical urge to move that is present independent of anxiety or mood symptoms. Symptoms began before age 12, have persisted into adulthood, occur across multiple settings (work meetings, calls), and cause functional impairment/embarrassment, consistent with ADHD, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation.
